gap: The app-internal claim is answered in the wrong statistic and is false as written. REFERENCE §5.3's bar is "≤5 ms **average**, ≤16 ms **worst case**" (Fatin's Typometer figures are means: Notepad++ 4.3, Emacs 5.3, Sublime 8.2). The report answers it with p50 5.67 and p99 14.99 and prints "The application's own work is inside the ≤5 ms / ≤16 ms bar". Recomputing the mean from the shipped raw samples in `/home/diggle/Work/wisprflowcopy/shots/latency/r2-appcost.json` gives 6.94 ms for prose_end_of_draft and 6.3–7.5 ms for *every* paced regime (fast_typist 7.52, focus_sentence 7.38), and the worst keystroke of prose_end is 17.34 ms. So the honest reading is ~6.9 ms mean / 17.3 ms worst — Emacs-to-Sublime class, real, defensible, and **over** the stated bar on both terms. Substituting p50 for mean and p99 for worst is the same apples-to-oranges the round-1 critique killed, moved down one level. Fix: restate §6 and the summary table in means and worsts, then close the ~2 ms — the 2,510 µs of style/layout/paint and the 1,414 µs Chrome textarea insertion per key are where it is, not in Quill's own 814 µs handler.
verdict: The methodology is genuinely better than almost anything published in this space — 10k-word real document, three sessions of 300 keys, every keydown asserted against trace and in-page probe with one failing run actually withheld, EventTiming presentation feedback rather than a rAF guess, bootstrap CIs on p99, CPU throttling, a four-size sweep, a 2,500-keystroke session, cold launcher runs and raw samples shipped. But it does not clear the bar it says it clears: the app-internal mean is 6.9 ms against a ≤5 ms mean bar and the worst is 17.3 ms against ≤16, and the report calls that "inside the bar" by quoting p50/p99 instead. The photon headline of 27.6 ms beats Hume's 32.5 at the median (and at the mean, 25.9 — I checked), but it is a measurement plus a cited 4 ms, taken entirely on a virtual Hyprland output whose commit→present hop the authors themselves say may be a whole refresh interval wrong in either direction — an uncertainty larger than the 5 ms margin to the bar — and the p99 of 41.7 is admitted to be the VS Code bracket. Strong work, one round short: on a 55k-word manuscript it is 16.9 ms of main-thread work per keystroke, and the caret the writer is actually watching still arrives 58 ms after the glyph.

builderNote: Rewrote tools/latency.mjs around round 1's verdict: twelve regimes of scripted real prose (capitals, punctuation, Enter, Backspace, undo, Ctrl+V paste, select-and-replace, Markdown fences) with every keystroke labelled by kind, a fresh page per regime so the double-probe bug is unrepresentable, three sessions with bootstrap p99 intervals, 2×/4× CPU throttling, four document sizes, a 2,500-keystroke session, an idle frame-production control, and true cold starts that spawn a browser process per run; bin/quill now measures on a virtual Hyprland output so a real compositor presents the frames without touching the user's screen. core.js perf: no data-i renumbering, one tokenise per changed line instead of two, and the re-tokenising below an edit bounded by what is on screen (a fence-opening keystroke in a 55k-word document: render() 26.16 → 3.33 ms). Measured: application's own work 5.7 ms p50 / 15.0 p99 (4.8 to a committed frame, 814 µs of it ours), 23.6 / 37.7 ms on the compositor, 375 ms from a shell to the document on screen — and the report says plainly where we are over the bar (55k words, 4× slower CPU, and the p99 photon figure).
secondary: No physical panel was measured at all this round, so the entire headline number rests on a virtual Hyprland output. Its commit→present hop measures 17.33 ms p50; round 1's single physical-panel session (older build) measured 5.0 ms. That ±12 ms of uncertainty is larger than the 5 ms margin by which 27.6 beats 32.5 — the headline could honestly be 18 ms or could be worse, and nothing in this round distinguishes them. The report says the panel run takes ten minutes on a free workspace; it was not run.

The photon arithmetic is missing an input term, not just the keyboard. Keys are injected with CDP `Input.dispatchKeyEvent`, so the clock starts inside the browser process: kernel/libinput/compositor→client delivery is excluded entirely. §13 justifies excluding any input term because Hume used a 1 kHz USB emulator — but that emulator only removes keyboard debounce and polling, not macOS's event delivery to the app, which is inside Hume's 32.5 ms. Ours is optimistic by an unquantified few ms.

The fence-flip win is largely work moved, not removed. `AHEAD=64` lines are tokenised inside the keystroke and the remainder (~3,200 lines in doc52k) is caught up in rAF chunks of 400 — roughly eight frames of unmeasured main-thread work immediately after the key. The 26.16 → 3.33 ms before/after in §14 prices only the synchronous part; the cost and frame-drop behaviour of the catch-up frames is measured nowhere.

`Writer.flushPending()` has zero callers anywhere in app/, tools/ or bin/ (grepped). So "nothing the reader can see is ever stale" holds only if the reader does not scroll during the ~130 ms catch-up window — there is no flush on scroll, and the correctness probe deliberately samples a line 400 below the fold, then sleeps 400 ms before checking it. AHEAD=64 is also asserted as "more than a screenful at any font size" rather than measured; at the small end of the size range in a 1440-logical-px-tall window on the user's own 4K panel it is closer to one screenful than two.

The startup headline is the pre-paint number. `startup_ready: 322` is `window.__quillReady`, a JS marker set at the end of `Writer.boot()` — before any frame exists. The first frame a human sees is 375 ms (351–377), and the true first run is 380 ms. Quoting 322 as "an editor you can type into" is the smaller of the two numbers, and it is the one that got promoted to the top level of latency.json.

Cold launcher n = 4 (and n = 3 fresh). Every other table in this report carries 900 samples and a bootstrap CI; the startup claim that is actually about the shipped product carries four runs and a min–max range.

The top-level `keystroke_p50` / `keystroke_p99` in latency.json are synthetic (23.64 + 4 cited, 37.70 + 4 cited). Any tile or downstream consumer reading those two fields gets a partly-cited number presented as measured; the disclosure lives in a sibling `bar_note` string that consumers will not render.

Variance is 2.5× the bar's. Pooled compositor prose_end is mean 21.90, sd 10.21 (I recomputed from r2-headed-{1,2,3}.json); Hume's Sublime is 32.5 ± 4.0. Same centre, much wider spread — jitter a writer feels, and it is reported only as p50/p90/p99, never as sd beside Hume's sd.

Several by-key-type cells are noise reported as statistics: undo n = 2 (a "p99" of 16.66 from two samples), capital n = 4–5 with a p99 equal to its max. §8's tables print p99 and worst for all of them.

The two places the app plainly loses are stated but not fixed and not in the headline: a 55k-word manuscript costs 16.9 ms of main-thread work per keystroke (one whole frame) with an app-only p99 of 21.7 ms, and at 4× CPU throttle the 10k document falls to 20.3 ms p50 with only 17% of keystrokes inside one frame. The tiles quote the 10k, full-speed, best-case row.

The caret — the thing a typist's eye is actually on — lags the glyph by 57.7 ms p50 at 133 wpm and is excluded from every table by construction. Against Dan Luu's 2 ms perception threshold that is the largest perceptible latency in the product, and it is filed as design rather than counted.
